claims.claim: Bumble bee male marking pheromone fatty alcohols are presumed to be biosynthesized by some of the numerous bumble bee FAR gene family members.
claims.source: which are presumed to be biosynthesized by some of the numerous bumble bee FAR gene family members (Buček et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on bumble bee FARs.

claims.claim: Bumble bee males employ MMPs to attract conspecific virgin queens.
claims.source: Bumble bee males employ MMPs to attract conspecific virgin queens (Goulson, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on bumble bee mating behavior.

claims.claim: MMP fatty alcohols consist predominantly of saturated, mono-unsaturated and poly-unsaturated fatty alcohols with 16–18 carbon atoms.
claims.source: MMP fatty alcohols consist predominantly of saturated, mono-unsaturated and poly-unsaturated fatty alcohols with 16–18 carbon atoms (Ayasse and Jarau, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on bumble bee pheromone composition.

claims.claim: Fatty alcohols are the major compounds in MMPs of B. lapidarius (hexadecanol and Z9-hexadecenol).
claims.source: Fatty alcohols are the major compounds in MMPs of B. lapidarius (hexadecanol and Z9-hexadecenol) and accompany electroantennogram-active compounds in B. terrestris (hexadecanol, octadecatrienol, octadecenol) and B. lucorum (hexadecanol, Z9,Z12-octadecadienol, Z9,Z12,Z15-octadecatrienol, octadecanol) (Bergström et al., 1973; Kullenberg et al., 1973; Kullenberg et al., 1970; Urbanová et al., 2001; Sobotník et al., 2008; Luxová et al., 2003; Zácek et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on bumble bee pheromone composition.

claims.claim: The substrate specificities of fatty acyl desaturases (FADs) are conserved across bumble bee species despite differences in the compositions of their unsaturated FA-derived pheromone components.
claims.source: In our previous investigation of the molecular basis of pheromone diversity in bumble bees, we found that the substrate specificities of fatty acyl desaturases (FADs), enzymes presumably acting upstream of FARs in pheromone biosynthesis (Tillman et al., 1999), are conserved across species despite differences in the compositions of their unsaturated FA-derived pheromone components (Buček et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on bumble bee FADs.

claims.claim: The substrate specificity of FADs contributes only partially to the species-specific composition of FA-derived MMPs in bumble bees.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the substrate specificity of FADs contributes only partially to the species-specific composition of FA-derived MMPs (Buček et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous work on bumble bee FADs.

claims.claim: The fatty alcohol content in bumble bee MMPs is presumably co-determined by the enzymatic specificity of other pheromone biosynthetic steps, such as FA biosynthesis/transport or FA reduction.
claims.source: The fatty alcohol content in bumble bee MMPs is therefore presumably co-determined by the enzymatic specificity of other pheromone biosynthetic steps, such as FA biosynthesis/transport or FA reduction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that FAD specificity alone does not explain pheromone composition.

claims.claim: Analysis of the B. terrestris male labial gland (LG) transcriptome uncovered a remarkably high number of putative FAR paralogs.
claims.source: Analysis of the B. terrestris male labial gland (LG) transcriptome uncovered a remarkably high number of putative FAR paralogs, including apparently expressed pseudogenes, strongly indicating dynamic evolution of the FAR gene family and the contribution of FARs to the LG-localized MMP biosynthesis (Buček et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous transcriptome analysis work.

claims.claim: The B. terrestris male labial gland transcriptome includes apparently expressed FAR pseudogenes.
claims.source: Analysis of the B. terrestris male labial gland (LG) transcriptome uncovered a remarkably high number of putative FAR paralogs, including apparently expressed pseudogenes, strongly indicating dynamic evolution of the FAR gene family and the contribution of FARs to the LG-localized MMP biosynthesis (Buček et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous transcriptome analysis work.

claims.claim: Searches for FAR-coding transcripts in the LG and FB transcriptomes yielded 12, 26 and 16 expressed FAR homologs in B. lapidarius, B. terrestris and B. lucorum, respectively.
claims.source: Searches for FAR-coding transcripts in the LG and FB transcriptomes of B. lapidarius and the previously sequenced FB and LG transcriptomes of B. lucorum and B. terrestris (Buček et al., 2013; Prchalová et al., 2016) yielded 12, 26 and 16 expressed FAR homologs in B. lapidarius, B. terrestris and B. lucorum, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptome sequencing and analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Eleven FAR ortholog groups (FAR-A to FAR-K) were retrieved as branches with high bootstrap support in the FAR gene tree.
claims.source: We assigned the names FAR-A to FAR-K to 11 FAR ortholog groups that were retrieved as branches with high bootstrap support in the FAR gene tree.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: FAR ortholog groups typically encompass one or more FARs from each of the hymenopteran species used in the tree inference, with the exception of apparent species-specific FAR duplications or losses.
claims.source: These ortholog groups typically encompass one or more FARs from each of the hymenopteran species used in the tree inference, with the exception of apparent species-specific FAR duplications or losses (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and visual inspection of the gene tree.

claims.claim: A massive expansion of the FAR-A ortholog group occurred in the bumble bee and stingless bee (subfamily Meliponini) sister lineages.
claims.source: Notably, we identified a massive expansion of the FAR-A ortholog group in the bumble bee and stingless bee (subfamily Meliponini) sister lineages (Figure 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing many FAR-A genes in these lineages.

claims.claim: The number of FAR homologs is inflated by a large number of predicted FAR genes and FAR transcripts with incomplete protein coding sequences lacking catalytically critical regions.
claims.source: The number of FAR homologs is inflated by a large number of predicted FAR genes and FAR transcripts with incomplete protein coding sequences lacking catalytically critical regions, such as the putative active site, NAD(P)+ binding site or substrate binding site (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by conserved domain analysis of predicted FAR sequences.

claims.claim: The FAR gene tree indicates expansion of the FAR-A ortholog group in the ant Camponotus floridanus and the mining bee Andrena vaga.
claims.source: The FAR gene tree also indicates expansion of the FAR-A ortholog group in the ant Camponotus floridanus and the mining bee Andrena vaga.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing multiple FAR-A genes in these species.

claims.claim: FAR-A expansion is not present in two other ant species (Acromyrmex echinatior and Harpegnathos saltator) and two other mining bee species (Andrenidae: Camptopoeum sacrum and Panurgus dentipes).
claims.source: However, this expansion is not present in two other ant species (Acromyrmex echinatior and Harpegnathos saltator) and two other mining bee species (Andrenidae: Camptopoeum sacrum and Panurgus dentipes) (Figure 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing single or few FAR-A genes in these species.

claims.claim: Extensive FAR-B gene expansion occurred in ants (Formicoidea).
claims.source: Several additional expansions of FAR families can be inferred from the FAR gene tree, including extensive FAR-B gene expansion in ants (Formicoidea), along with many more lineage-specific FAR gene duplications and minor expansions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing multiple FAR-B genes in ant species.

claims.claim: The Drosophila melanogaster Waterproof FAR was placed in the FAR-J ortholog group.
claims.source: The only functionally characterized FAR from D. melanogaster—Waterproof (NP_651652.2), which is involved in the biosynthesis of a protective wax layer (Jaspers et al., 2014)—was placed in the FAR-J ortholog group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis including non-hymenopteran insect FARs.

claims.claim: The FAR-G ortholog group includes a FAR gene from Apis mellifera with unclear biological function and a sex pheromone-biosynthetic FAR from B. mori.
claims.source: The FAR-G ortholog group includes a FAR gene from Apis mellifera with unclear biological function (Teerawanichpan et al., 2010b) and a sex pheromone-biosynthetic FAR from B. mori (Moto et al., 2003) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to literature on these FARs.

claims.claim: The majority of FAR ortholog groups contain predicted FARs from both hymenopteran and non-hymenopteran insect species.
claims.source: In the gene tree, the majority of FAR ortholog groups contain predicted FARs from both hymenopteran and non-hymenopteran insect species, although the bootstrap support is <80% for some FAR groups.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis including diverse insect species.

claims.claim: The presence of FAR ortholog groups in representatives of Hymenoptera, Coleoptera, Lepidoptera and Diptera indicates that these groups are ancestral to holometabolous insects.
claims.source: The presence of these FAR ortholog groups in representatives of Hymenoptera, Coleoptera, Lepidoptera and Diptera indicates that these groups are ancestral to holometabolous insects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic distribution of FAR ortholog groups.

claims.claim: FAR-D is the only FAR group that does not include any non-hymenopteran FARs from the dataset.
claims.source: FAR-D is the only FAR group that does not include any non-hymenopteran FARs from our dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and thus presumably represents Hymenoptera-specific FAR gene family expansions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing FAR-D only in hymenopteran species.

claims.claim: FAR-D presumably represents Hymenoptera-specific FAR gene family expansions.
claims.source: FAR-D is the only FAR group that does not include any non-hymenopteran FARs from our dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and thus presumably represents Hymenoptera-specific FAR gene family expansions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of FAR-D.

claims.claim: FAR-Ds do not contain the complete set of three catalytically critical regions and their enzymatic role is unclear.
claims.source: FAR-Ds, however, do not contain the complete set of three catalytically critical regions (i.e. the putative active site, NAD(P)+ binding site and substrate binding site) and their enzymatic role is therefore unclear.
claims.evidence: This is supported by conserved domain analysis of FAR-D sequences.

claims.claim: The majority of FAR genes belonging to the non-FAR-A gene ortholog group localize to the B. terrestris genome assembled to linkage groups.
claims.source: While the majority of FAR genes belonging to the non-FAR-A gene ortholog group localize to the B. terrestris genome assembled to linkage groups, most of the B. terrestris FAR-A genes localize to unlinked short scaffolds (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of FAR gene positions in the B. terrestris genome assembly.

claims.claim: Most of the B. terrestris FAR-A genes localize to unlinked short scaffolds.
claims.source: While the majority of FAR genes belonging to the non-FAR-A gene ortholog group localize to the B. terrestris genome assembled to linkage groups, most of the B. terrestris FAR-A genes localize to unlinked short scaffolds (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of FAR gene positions in the B. terrestris genome assembly.

claims.claim: Some of the FAR-A genes in the B. terrestris genome are arranged in clusters.
claims.source: Some of the FAR-A genes in the B. terrestris genome are arranged in clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of FAR gene positions in genome scaffolds.

claims.claim: TEs are significantly enriched around FAR-A genes compared to the genome-wide average around randomly selected genes in B. terrestris.
claims.source: Our analysis of the distribution of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes in the B. terrestris and B. impatiens genomes confirmed that TEs are significantly enriched around FAR-A genes compared to the genome-wide average around randomly selected genes (Figure 3AC; B. terrestris: p < 0.0001, B. impatiens: p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TE density around FAR genes.

claims.claim: TEs are significantly enriched around FAR-A genes compared to the genome-wide average around randomly selected genes in B. impatiens.
claims.source: Our analysis of the distribution of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes in the B. terrestris and B. impatiens genomes confirmed that TEs are significantly enriched around FAR-A genes compared to the genome-wide average around randomly selected genes (Figure 3AC; B. terrestris: p < 0.0001, B. impatiens: p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TE density around FAR genes.

claims.claim: More than 50% of the 10 kb regions surrounding FAR-A genes are formed by TEs, compared to an average of 10% around randomly selected B. terrestris genes.
claims.source: On average, more than 50% of the 10 kb regions surrounding FAR-A genes are formed by TEs, compared to an average of 10% around randomly selected B. terrestris genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of TE density around FAR genes.

claims.claim: The densities of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes not belonging to the FAR-A group do not differ from the genome-wide average in B. terrestris.
claims.source: In contrast, the densities of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes not belonging to the FAR-A group do not differ from the genome-wide average (Figure 3AC; B. terrestris: p = 0.793; B. impatiens: p = 0.880).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TE density around non-FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: The densities of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes not belonging to the FAR-A group do not differ from the genome-wide average in B. impatiens.
claims.source: In contrast, the densities of TEs in the vicinity of FAR genes not belonging to the FAR-A group do not differ from the genome-wide average (Figure 3AC; B. terrestris: p = 0.793; B. impatiens: p = 0.880).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TE density around non-FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: There is a statistically significant difference in TE densities between FAR-A genes and non-FAR-A genes in B. terrestris.
claims.source: Also, there is a statistically significant difference in TE densities between FAR-A genes and non-FAR-A genes (Man-Whitney U-test: B. terrestris: U = 167, p < 0.0001; B. impatiens: U = 78, p = 0.0002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of TE densities between FAR-A and non-FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: There is a statistically significant difference in TE densities between FAR-A genes and non-FAR-A genes in B. impatiens.
claims.source: Also, there is a statistically significant difference in TE densities between FAR-A genes and non-FAR-A genes (Man-Whitney U-test: B. terrestris: U = 167, p < 0.0001; B. impatiens: U = 78, p = 0.0002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of TE densities between FAR-A and non-FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: All major known TE families are statistically enriched in the neighborhood of the FAR-A genes.
claims.source: Although all major known TE families are statistically enriched in the neighborhood of the FAR-A genes (Figure 3BD), the Class I comprising retroid elements contributes considerably to the elevated repeat content around FAR-A genes (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of individual TE family densities around FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: Class I retroid elements contribute considerably to the elevated repeat content around FAR-A genes.
claims.source: Although all major known TE families are statistically enriched in the neighborhood of the FAR-A genes (Figure 3BD), the Class I comprising retroid elements contributes considerably to the elevated repeat content around FAR-A genes (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of TE class contributions to enrichment around FAR-A genes.

claims.claim: Ten promising MMP-biosynthetic FAR candidates were among the 100 most abundant transcripts in the LG and were substantially more abundant in LG than in FB based on RNA-Seq-derived normalized expression values.
claims.source: We selected 10 promising MMP-biosynthetic FAR candidates that were (1) among the 100 most abundant transcripts in the LG and were substantially more abundant in LG than in FB based on RNA-Seq-derived normalized expression values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and ref. (Buček et al., 2016))
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq expression analysis data.

claims.claim: The ten selected FAR candidates included all the predicted catalytically critical regions of FARs.
claims.source: and (2) included all the predicted catalytically critical regions of FARs—the putative active site, NAD(P)+ binding site and substrate binding site in the protein coding sequence (Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by conserved domain analysis of FAR sequences.

claims.claim: The FAR candidates follow a general trend of overexpression in male LG compared to FB, flight muscle and gut.
claims.source: By employing reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) on an expanded set of bumble bee tissues, we confirmed that the FAR candidates follow a general trend of overexpression in male LG compared to FB, flight muscle and gut (all from male bumble bees) and virgin queen LG (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR expression analysis data.

claims.claim: B. lapidarius FAR-A1 (BlapFAR-A1) transcripts are abundant in virgin queen LG at levels comparable to those in male LG.
claims.source: Notably, B. lapidarius FAR-A1 (BlapFAR-A1) and B. terrestris FAR-J (BterFAR-J) transcripts are also abundant in virgin queen LG, where they are expressed at levels comparable to those in male LG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR expression analysis data.

claims.claim: B. terrestris FAR-J (BterFAR-J) transcripts are abundant in virgin queen LG at levels comparable to those in male LG.
claims.source: Notably, B. lapidarius FAR-A1 (BlapFAR-A1) and B. terrestris FAR-J (BterFAR-J) transcripts are also abundant in virgin queen LG, where they are expressed at levels comparable to those in male LG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR expression analysis data.

claims.claim: In the LGs, 4, 14 and 19 individual fatty alcohol compounds were detected in B. lapidarius, B. lucorum and B. terrestris, respectively.
claims.source: In the LGs, we detected 4, 14 and 19 individual fatty alcohol compounds in B. lapidarius, B. lucorum and B. terrestris, respectively (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols in bumble bee LGs.

claims.claim: A limited number of fatty alcohols (mainly 16:OH, Z9,Z12-18:OH and Z9,Z12,Z15-18:OH) were detected in FBs of B. lucorum and B. terrestris, but at substantially lower abundance than in LGs.
claims.source: A limited number of fatty alcohols (mainly 16:OH, Z9,Z12-18:OH and Z9,Z12,Z15-18:OH) also were detected in FBs of B. lucorum and B. terrestris, but at substantially lower abundance than in LGs (Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols in bumble bee FBs.

claims.claim: Fatty alcohol ratios are greater than 50% for most of the fatty alcohols in LGs.
claims.source: These ratios are greater than 50% for most of the fatty alcohols in LGs and even approach 100% for some of the monounsaturated >C20 fatty alcohols, suggesting high overall conversion rates of acyl substrates to alcohols.
claims.evidence: This is supported by calculation of fatty alcohol ratios from GC quantification data.

claims.claim: Fatty alcohol ratios approach 100% for some of the monounsaturated >C20 fatty alcohols in LGs, suggesting high overall conversion rates of acyl substrates to alcohols.
claims.source: These ratios are greater than 50% for most of the fatty alcohols in LGs and even approach 100% for some of the monounsaturated >C20 fatty alcohols, suggesting high overall conversion rates of acyl substrates to alcohols.
claims.evidence: This is supported by calculation of fatty alcohol ratios from GC quantification data and represents an inference about enzymatic conversion efficiency.

claims.claim: FARs from three bumble bee species belonging to the FAR-J ortholog group share 97.2–99.7% protein sequence identity.
claims.source: FARs from three bumble bee species belonging to the FAR-J ortholog group are nearly identical, sharing 97.2–99.7% protein sequence identity
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein sequence comparison analysis.

claims.claim: BlucFAR-A1 and BterFAR-A1 share 99.4% protein sequence identity with each other and 60.9–61.1% with BlapFAR-A1.
claims.source: BlucFAR-A1 and BterFAR-A1 share 99.4% protein sequence identity with each other and 60.9–61.1% with BlapFAR-A1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein sequence comparison analysis.

claims.claim: BlucFAR-A2 and BterFAR-A2 share 94.8% protein sequence identity.
claims.source: BlucFAR-A2 and BterFAR-A2 share 94.8% protein sequence identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein sequence comparison analysis.

claims.claim: BlapFAR-A1-short has an in-frame internal 66 bp deletion in the coding region that does not disrupt the predicted active site, putative NAD(P)+ binding site or putative substrate binding site.
claims.source: BlapFAR-A1-short has an in-frame internal 66 bp deletion in the coding region that does not disrupt the predicted active site, putative NAD(P)+ binding site or putative substrate binding site (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and conserved domain prediction.

claims.claim: Both BlapFAR-A1 and BlapFAR-A1-short are expressed in the B. lapidarius male LG and virgin queen LG.
claims.source: Using RT-qPCR with specific primers for each variant, we confirmed that both BlapFAR-A1 and BlapFAR-A1-short are expressed in the B. lapidarius male LG and virgin queen LG (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR expression analysis data.

claims.claim: His-tagged FARs were detected in all yeast strains transformed with plasmids bearing FARs.
claims.source: His-tagged FARs were detected in all yeast strains transformed with plasmids bearing FARs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while no His-tagged proteins were detected in the negative control (yeasts transformed with an empty plasmid).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of yeast protein extracts.

claims.claim: No His-tagged proteins were detected in the negative control (yeasts transformed with an empty plasmid).
claims.source: His-tagged FARs were detected in all yeast strains transformed with plasmids bearing FARs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while no His-tagged proteins were detected in the negative control (yeasts transformed with an empty plasmid).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of yeast protein extracts.

claims.claim: The synthetic BlucFAR-A1-opt and BlucFAR-A2-opt coding regions with codon usage optimized for S. cerevisiae showed a single major western blot signal corresponding to the position of the predicted full-length protein.
claims.source: The synthetic BlucFAR-A1-opt and BlucFAR-A2-opt coding regions with codon usage optimized for S. cerevisiae showed a single major western blot signal corresponding to the position of the predicted full-length protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of yeast protein extracts.

claims.claim: The shortened heterologously expressed proteins presumably represent incompletely transcribed versions of full-length FARs resulting from ribosome stalling.
claims.source: The shortened heterologously expressed proteins thus presumably represent incompletely transcribed versions of full-length FARs resulting from ribosome stalling (Angov, 2011)
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on western blot patterns and citation to literature on ribosome stalling.

claims.claim: The higher molecular weight bands in western blots might correspond to aggregates of full-length and incompletely translated FARs.
claims.source: while the higher molecular weight bands might correspond to aggregates of full-length and incompletely translated FARs.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on western blot patterns.

claims.claim: The codon-optimized BlucFAR-A1-opt and BlucFAR-A2-opt exhibit the same overall specificity in yeast expression system as the respective non-codon-optimized FARs.
claims.source: Because the codon-optimized BlucFAR-A1-opt and BlucFAR-A2-opt exhibit the same overall specificity in yeast expression system as the respective non-codon-optimized FARs (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of fatty alcohol production profiles in yeast expressing optimized and non-optimized FARs.

claims.claim: Saturated C16 to C26 fatty alcohols are produced by both BterFAR-A1 and BlucFAR-A1 and BterFAR-J enzymes.
claims.source: Functional characterization of FARs from B. terrestris and B. lucorum in yeast indicated that saturated C16 to C26 fatty alcohols are produced by both BterFAR-A1 and BlucFAR-A1 and BterFAR-J enzymes (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing these FARs.

claims.claim: Bter/BlucFAR-A1 prefers C22 substrates.
claims.source: Bter/BlucFAR-A1 prefers C22 substrates, whereas BterFAR-J has an optimal substrate preference slightly shifted to C24.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fatty alcohol production profiles in yeast.

claims.claim: BterFAR-J has an optimal substrate preference slightly shifted to C24.
claims.source: Bter/BlucFAR-A1 prefers C22 substrates, whereas BterFAR-J has an optimal substrate preference slightly shifted to C24.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fatty alcohol production profiles in yeast.

claims.claim: BterFAR-A1 and BlucFAR-A1 are capable of reducing supplemented monounsaturated Z15-20: acyl to the corresponding alcohol.
claims.source: Unlike any of the other characterized FARs, BterFAR-A1 and BlucFAR-A1 are also capable of reducing supplemented monounsaturated Z15-20: acyl to the corresponding alcohol (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing these FARs and supplemented with Z15-20: acyl.

claims.claim: Both BterFAR-A2 and BlucFAR-A2 reduce only 16: and 18: acyls.
claims.source: Both BterFAR-A2 and BlucFAR-A2 reduce only 16: and 18: acyls (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing these FARs.

claims.claim: BlapFAR-A1 produces Z9-16:OH and Z9-18:OH.
claims.source: Characterization of B. lapidarius FARs showed that BlapFAR-A1, in contrast to BterFAR-A1 and BlucFAR-A1, produces Z9-16:OH and Z9-18:OH (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing BlapFAR-A1.

claims.claim: BlapFAR-A4 produces 16:OH and Z9-16:OH, together with lower quantities of 14:OH and Z9-18:OH.
claims.source: BlapFAR-A4 produces 16:OH and Z9-16:OH, together with lower quantities of 14:OH and Z9-18:OH (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 8A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing BlapFAR-A4.

claims.claim: BlapFAR-A5 produces 16:OH as a major product and lower amounts of 14:OH, Z9-16:OH, 18:OH and Z9-18:OH.
claims.source: BlapFAR-A5 produces 16:OH as a major product and lower amounts of 14:OH, Z9-16:OH, 18:OH and Z9-18:OH (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 8A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing BlapFAR-A5.

claims.claim: Both BlapFAR-A1 and BlapFAR-A4 are capable of reducing supplemented polyunsaturated fatty acyls (Z9,Z12-18: and Z9,Z12,Z15-18:) to their respective alcohols.
claims.source: In addition, both BlapFAR-A1 and BlapFAR-A4 are capable of reducing supplemented polyunsaturated fatty acyls (Z9,Z12-18: and Z9,Z12,Z15-18:) to their respective alcohols (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 6AB).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing these FARs and supplemented with polyunsaturated acyls.

claims.claim: BlapFAR-J reduces saturated C16 to C26 acyls.
claims.source: Similarly to BterFAR-J, BlapFAR-J also reduces saturated C16 to C26 acyls (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of fatty alcohols produced in yeast expressing BlapFAR-J.

claims.claim: No fatty alcohols were detected in the negative control (yeasts transformed with empty plasmid).
claims.source: No fatty alcohols were detected in the negative control, that is the yeasts transformed with empty plasmid (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC analysis of lipid extracts from control yeast cultures.

claims.claim: The total quantities of fatty alcohols accumulated in FAR-expressing yeasts range from few milligrams to tens of milligrams per liter of culture.
claims.source: The total quantities of fatty alcohols accumulated in FAR-expressing yeasts range from few milligrams to tens of milligrams per liter of culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 8B), the exceptions being BterFAR-A2 and BlucFAR-A2 which both produce sub-milligram quantities of fatty alcohols.

results.result: A massive expansion of the FAR-A ortholog group occurred in the common ancestor of bumble bees (Bombini) and stingless bees (Meliponini) after their divergence from Apis approximately 54 million years ago. This expansion was a highly dynamic process characterized by numerous gene duplications, losses, and pseudogenization events.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C6, C42, C104, C105, C106, C108, C109, and C136 are well-supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1, Figure 2) showing FAR-A expansion in both bumble bee and stingless bee lineages but not in their sister groups. The presence of numerous pseudogenes (C106, C108) and species-specific duplications/losses (C109) supports the dynamic nature of this expansion. The timing estimate (C105) is based on published phylogenetic dating.

results.result: Transposable elements (TEs) are significantly enriched around FAR-A genes compared to genome-wide averages and non-FAR-A genes in both B. terrestris and B. impatiens genomes, with Class I retroid elements contributing considerably to this enrichment. This TE enrichment presumably facilitated the massive FAR-A expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C57-C65, C123, and C138 are supported by statistical analysis of TE density (Figure 3) showing significant enrichment (p < 0.0001) around FAR-A genes in both species, with >50% of 10 kb regions surrounding FAR-A genes formed by TEs compared to ~10% genome-wide average. The causal link between TE enrichment and FAR expansion (C5, C123, C138) is presented as an inference ('presumably'), which is appropriately cautious given the correlational nature of the evidence.

results.result: Bumble bee FARs from the expanded FAR-A ortholog group, along with FAR-J, contribute to species-specific male marking pheromone (MMP) composition through their distinct substrate specificities. The characterized FARs show LG-specific expression and produce fatty alcohols that correlate with MMP composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C66-C68, C86-C95, C102, C134-C135, C139-C142, and C155 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) RT-qPCR showing LG-specific expression (Figure 4, C68), (2) functional characterization in yeast demonstrating distinct substrate specificities (Figure 6, C86-C95), and (3) correlation between FAR specificities and MMP composition (Figure 5, C102, C139-C142). The combined evidence from expression, functional assays, and chemical analysis provides strong support for the role of FAR-A genes in MMP biosynthesis.

results.result: Expansion and functional diversification of the FAR gene family played a key role in the evolution of pheromone communication in Hymenoptera, particularly in bumble bees and stingless bees where FAR-A expansion correlates with the use of fatty alcohols as marking pheromones.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C112, and C137 represent the main conclusion of the manuscript. This conclusion is supported by the convergence of multiple results: (1) FAR-A expansion in bumble bees and stingless bees (C4, C6, C42), (2) both lineages use LG-produced fatty alcohols as marking pheromones (C110, C111), (3) characterized FAR-A enzymes produce fatty alcohols found in MMPs (C7, C86-C95), and (4) FAR specificities correlate with species-specific MMP composition (C139-C142). The correlation between FAR expansion and pheromone use provides strong support for this evolutionary inference.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis identified 11 FAR ortholog groups (FAR-A to FAR-K) across Hymenoptera, with most groups ancestral to holometabolous insects. FAR-D appears to be Hymenoptera-specific, and additional expansions occurred in specific lineages (e.g., FAR-B in ants).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41, C43-C46, C49-C52 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing 11 ortholog groups with high bootstrap support. The presence of these groups across multiple insect orders (C49, C50) supports their ancestral origin. The Hymenoptera-specific nature of FAR-D (C51, C52) is supported by its absence in non-hymenopteran species in the dataset, though this inference is limited by taxonomic sampling.

results.result: Most B. terrestris FAR-A genes localize to unlinked short scaffolds in the genome assembly, with some arranged in clusters, while non-FAR-A genes typically localize to assembled linkage groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by analysis of FAR gene positions in the B. terrestris genome assembly (Supplementary file 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The localization of FAR-A genes to short scaffolds is consistent with their location in repetitive, TE-rich regions that are difficult to assemble. However, this result is limited by the quality of the genome assembly and does not provide information about the actual chromosomal organization of FAR-A genes.

results.result: BlapFAR-A1 and BterFAR-J are abundantly expressed in both male and virgin queen labial glands at comparable levels, suggesting potential roles in queen-specific signal production.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C70, and C79 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing expression in both male and queen LGs. However, the inference that these FARs are involved in queen-specific signal production (C156) is speculative and not directly tested. The expression pattern is consistent with this hypothesis, but functional evidence linking these FARs to queen signals is lacking.

results.result: Comprehensive GC analysis revealed species-specific fatty alcohol profiles in bumble bee male LGs, with fatty alcohol ratios >50% for most compounds, suggesting high conversion rates. The composition of LG fatty acyls contributes substantially to final MMP composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74, C143-C145 are supported by GC analysis data (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing detailed fatty alcohol and fatty acyl profiles. The high fatty alcohol ratios (C73, C74) provide evidence for efficient enzymatic conversion. The inference that substrate availability affects MMP composition (C143-C145) is supported by correlations between fatty acyl presence and fatty alcohol production, though direct experimental manipulation of substrate pools would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Characterized bumble bee FARs show high sequence identity within ortholog groups. BlapFAR-A1-short, a variant with a 66 bp in-frame deletion, is expressed but lacks detectable FAR activity, suggesting the deleted 22-amino acid region is necessary for enzymatic function.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78, C100-C101 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and functional characterization data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The high sequence identity within ortholog groups (C75-C77) is well-documented. The lack of activity in BlapFAR-A1-short (C100) despite expression and presence of conserved domains (C78) supports the inference that the deleted region is functionally important (C101), though the specific mechanism is not determined.

results.result: Heterologous expression of bumble bee FARs in yeast produced His-tagged proteins detected by western blot, with codon-optimized versions showing improved expression. All characterized FARs are strictly alcohol-forming, producing no detectable aldehydes, with total fatty alcohol yields ranging from sub-milligram to tens of milligrams per liter.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85, C96-C99 are supported by western blot analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and GC quantification data (Figure 6—figure supplement 8). The detection of His-tagged proteins (C80-C82) confirms expression, and the absence of fatty alcohols in negative controls (C96) validates the assay. The inference about ribosome stalling (C83) is reasonable based on the western blot patterns and literature citation, though alternative explanations for truncated proteins are possible. The strict alcohol-forming activity (C99) is well-supported by the absence of aldehyde detection.

results.result: None of the characterized FARs from B. lucorum or B. terrestris reduce polyunsaturated Z9,Z12-18: and Z9,Z12,Z15-18: acyls, despite these fatty alcohols being present in LGs. These fatty alcohols are also detected in fat body, suggesting a FAR capable of polyunsaturated acyl reduction might be expressed in both tissues and was missed by LG-specific selection criteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C103, C146-C149 are supported by functional characterization data showing no polyunsaturated fatty alcohol production by characterized FARs (C103) and GC analysis detecting these compounds in both LG and FB (C146, C72). The inference that a polyunsaturated acyl-reducing FAR was missed due to selection criteria (C148, C149) is reasonable given the LG-specific expression requirement used for candidate selection. However, this remains speculative without identification and characterization of such a FAR.

results.result: Discrepancies between FAR specificities in yeast and in vivo suggest that the composition of fatty acyl-CoA pools in bumble bee LGs differs from total fatty acyl pools. The selectivity of enzymes converting fatty acyls to fatty acyl-CoAs and protecting them from hydrolysis may represent an additional mechanism shaping species-specific fatty alcohol composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 identify important discrepancies between in vitro and in vivo FAR specificities (C150, C151) and propose a mechanistic explanation (C152-C154). While the discrepancies are well-documented by comparing yeast expression data with LG composition (Figure 5, Figure 6), the proposed mechanism involving differential fatty acyl-CoA pools (C152, C153) is speculative and not directly tested. The proposal about enzymes regulating fatty acyl-CoA pools (C154) is reasonable and supported by literature citations, but lacks direct experimental evidence in this system.

results.result: Bumble bee orthologs of B. mori pheromone-biosynthetic FAR (FAR-G) are not abundantly expressed in male bumble bee LGs, suggesting that MMP-biosynthetic FARs in bumble bees and sex pheromone-biosynthetic FARs in moths were recruited independently for pheromone biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C113 and C114 are supported by RNA-Seq expression data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing low FAR-G expression in bumble bee LGs and phylogenetic analysis showing different FAR ortholog groups involved in pheromone biosynthesis in these lineages. The inference of independent recruitment (C114) is well-supported by the phylogenetic distribution of pheromone-biosynthetic FARs across different ortholog groups in different insect orders.

results.result: Bumble bee males produce several milligrams of MMPs, orders of magnitude more than moth sex pheromones. Gene dosage benefits and sexual selection favoring males producing large MMP quantities could have contributed to FAR duplication and fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C115 and C116 are supported by quantitative data (Figure 5) and literature citation, respectively, establishing the large difference in pheromone quantities between bumble bees and moths. However, the speculation that gene dosage benefits (C117) and sexual selection (C118) drove FAR duplication is not directly tested. While this is a reasonable hypothesis consistent with gene duplication theory (supported by citations), it remains speculative without experimental evidence linking FAR copy number to MMP production levels or fitness.

results.result: Gene duplications can be facilitated by TEs, and similar TE-mediated expansions have been documented for FAD genes in Drosophila and Ostrinia. Several scenarios are proposed for how TEs might have facilitated FAR-A expansion in bumble bees, including a potential runaway process involving TE accumulation and gene family expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C119, C120, C122, C124, C125 are supported by literature citations establishing general principles of TE-mediated gene duplication and specific examples in other insect lineages. However, the specific scenarios proposed for FAR-A expansion (C126-C128, C131) are speculative and not directly tested. The Janoušek et al. model (C129, C130) provides a theoretical framework, but its applicability to bumble bee FAR-A expansion is not empirically validated. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further investigation.

results.result: The substrate specificity of FARs contributes to species-specific MMP composition, but other biosynthetic steps, particularly fatty acyl and fatty acyl-CoA accumulation, also likely contribute to the final fatty alcohol composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C132 and C133 represent a balanced conclusion supported by the combined evidence from FAR functional characterization (showing substrate specificity differences) and the observed discrepancies between in vitro FAR specificity and in vivo MMP composition. This conclusion appropriately acknowledges both the contribution of FAR specificity and the limitations in explaining all aspects of MMP composition through FAR specificity alone.

results.result: Background information and prior work establishing the biological roles of FARs and fatty alcohols, gene duplication as an evolutionary mechanism, FAR gene family characteristics across organisms, pheromone biosynthesis in moths and bumble bees, and previous findings on bumble bee FADs and FARs.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C38, C47-C48, C53, C110-C111 represent background knowledge and prior work that are appropriately cited and provide context for the current study. These claims are supported by citations to established literature and represent the state of knowledge in the field. They are not novel findings of this manuscript but are necessary for understanding the significance and context of the new results.
